Hi Rosa, it is Andres from the Santiago office. I am calling about the regional meeting. We have decided to move it to September, and I wanted you to hear it from me before the email goes out. I know the team was looking forward to meeting in Lima, and I am sorry about that. The problem is the budget. We simply cannot afford to fly twelve people in before the new fares are approved. I would suggest keeping the Thursday call as planned, because there are two clients who refuse to wait until September for an answer. And one more thing. Please remember to send me the revised proposal before Friday. Last time we managed to agree on everything in the room and then forgot to write it down. I do not want to make that mistake twice. Call me if you need anything.

Most meetings end with a decision, and most decisions die in the week after. In my experience, the problem is rarely the decision itself. It is that everybody agrees to do something and nobody arranges a time to do it. So here are three habits. First, before you leave the room, name the person who has agreed to act, and the date. Do not leave it as we should consider changing the process. Second, if you cannot afford the time this week, say so. Refusing politely is more professional than accepting and doing nothing. And third, admit mistakes early. A colleague who says I forgot to send the figures on Monday is easy to work with. A colleague who keeps promising to send them is not. Decisions do not fail in the meeting. They fail when people stop following up.
